📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association mentioned the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

It has been revealed that the move, which has yet to be publicly revealed by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow rolled out its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey.".

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there.".

Industry observers note that how this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been remarked about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days.".

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

"We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who mentioned he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

Recent findings suggest that "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place.".

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," stated spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius stated he didn't wish to "speculate on implications.".

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the problem could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

Duff has since taken charge and overseen seven league matches, with the Bantams winning two, drawing four and losing one of those while keeping five clean sheets to move onto a league-high tally of 10 for the season in 15 League One matches.

Following consecutive dominant cup victories, winning 7-0 and 4-0, and a 2-2 draw against Doncaster Rovers, the Bantams headed into a second straight Yorkshire Derby on Tuesday at home to Barnsley and dished out a 3-0 beating as Stephen Humphrys scored a brace and Jake Beesley added a late third from the spot.

Now back in the top six after a blip in the early stages under Duff, while boasting the league's best defensive record and having scored 16 goals in their last four matches to begin to remedy their attacking struggles, Bradford City will bid to make it consecutive wins on Saturday to close in on the automatic promotion spots.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, so where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Sources indicate that carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, mentioned he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Sources indicate that defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

Sources indicate that the strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

According to recent reports, chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

The problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

In a recent development, take nothing away from Morgan Rogers – his 40yd dash from the edge of the centre circle in United’s half to the six-yard box and the finish that followed were top notch. But where was the challenge? How could not a single player in red have stood in his path? “Come on Morgan, run through us buddy” seemed to be the message.

Michael Carrick remarked he expects to be in charge of Manchester United next week despite Lisandro Martinez’s moment of madness leaving the club mired in a relegation battle and on their worst run for 38 years.

In a recent development, it left United without a win in nine matches, their worst run since 1988, and at risk of being sucked into the relegation zone. They have won just two of 13 games this season.

Sources indicate that the Old Trafford hierarchy gave Carrick a stay of execution in midweek and, when asked if he expected to still to be at the helm when United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, the head coach replied: “Yes. I’m just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now.”.

It has been revealed that having been booked moments earlier for a foul on Morgan Rogers, Martinez was sent off for a second yellow. The incident came less than three weeks after the Argentinian was fined and publicly apologised for attacking United director of football Jason Wilcox and the board over transfer policy and was the latest in a series of mistakes from him on the pitch this season.

Joe Cole, the former Chelsea and England forward, believes United must get rid of Martinez.

In a recent development, “Whatever the next Manchester United looks like, Lisandro Martinez has run his course,’ Cole said on TNT Sports. “He’s at the scene of the crime too often for Manchester United and is at fault for moments and goals like that. So that’s probably his time done.”.

Carrick refused to publicly criticise Martinez but admitted his dismissal was a “huge moment” and felt his team “unravelled” in the second period.

Sources indicate that “Things have gone against us in a big way,” the United manager said. “It’s unravelled rapidly. There’s a lot of emotion right now. It’s a huge moment in the game. He’s gone to it and the referee gave that decision, but it’s a big moment.”.

Asked if there would be a stigma attached to United potentially dropping into the relegation zone, Carrick added: “Not for me, no.”.

And when asked how his players would deal with a relegation battle, Carrick added: “We’ve got to keep moving forward and winning games. There’s no words I’m going to explain to you now that makes any difference, it’s not going to change it. We’ve got to move forward and win matches.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Serie A disciplinary judge suspended no players after matchday 12, so neither Juventus nor Como lose anyone for Sunday's game.
  • It has been revealed that juventus travel to Como on Sunday with no suspension worries.
  • The decisions covered the games of 21, 22 and 23 November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Serie A disciplinary judge suspended no players after matchday 12, so neither Juventus nor Como lose anyone for Sunday's game. Como were fined again for a slow restart, and Juventus head to Lake Como five points behind them.

It has been revealed that juventus travel to Como on Sunday with no suspension worries. Nor do their hosts. Serie A disciplinary judge Gerardo Mastrandrea banned nobody after matchday 12 in a ruling published in Milan on 24 November.

The decisions covered the games of 21, 22 and 23 November. Nobody was sent off across the round. No player one booking from a ban picked up a yellow card either.

Industry observers note that juventus had no cards from their own fixture. The club’s match sheet for the 4-0 win over Venezia at the Allianz Stadium lists no bookings, with Arena as referee.

All four goals came after the break. Woltemade (53′), Koopmeiners (59′) and Cabal (65′) scored before Kolo Muani converted a penalty (71′).

Two Lecce players, Danilo Veiga and Jamil Siebert, picked up their fourth booking of the season and are now one caution from a ban, Virgilio Sport reported. No Juventus or Como player reached that threshold this round.

Como did not escape the judge entirely. The €8,000 fine was imposed under strict liability for delaying the start of the second half by about four minutes without good reason. The judge treated it as a repeated repeat offence.

Recent findings suggest that it was the largest of the round’s penalties for late restarts. Fiorentina and Milan were also fined as repeat offenders. Genoa received €3,000 for a two-minute delay to kick-off.

It has been revealed that the problem is not new for Como. In the previous round, the communiqué of 10 November fined them €10,000, again as repeated repeat offenders. On that occasion the second half started about two minutes late.

Juventus were not blameless that week. The same 10 November ruling fined them €5,000 for holding up the start of the first half by the same margin as Como’s latest delay.

The match carries weight in the race for the top four. Como have 8 wins, 2 draws and 2 defeats from their 12 games. They have scored 20 goals and conceded 10.

It has been revealed that juventus have 6 wins, 3 draws and 3 defeats. Their attack, with 19 goals, has almost kept pace with Como’s. The difference lies at the back, where Juventus have conceded 12.

A win on Lake Como would narrow the gap to their hosts. Defeat would push Juventus further from the top four.

Como host Juventus at the Sinigaglia on 29 November.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Anthony Nolan | 26 Nov 2026 22:39.

MEWA Arena will be the backdrop for a six-pointer in the lower reaches of the Bundesliga table, when Mainz 05 host relegation-threatened Union Berlin on Saturday.

Die Nullfunfer are desperate to avoid a sixth defeat on the bounce, while Die Eisernen are searching for their first win in six games.

Urs Fischer rescued Mainz when he took the reins midway through last season, but his team are at risk of being dragged into a fight for their survival this time around.

Die Nullfunfer were downed 3-1 by Augsburg last Sunday, falling three goals behind before finding a way through via substitute Ransford-Yeboah Konigsdorffer.

That defeat has left Fischer's side 13th in the Bundesliga table with just 10 points from their 10 matches, a tally that has the club sitting just three points above 16th-placed Schalke 04 - and their 17th-placed opponents - in the relegation zone.

Mainz arrive for Saturday's clash having lost each of their past five matches across all competitions, conceding 14 goals in the process with defending that the manager described as "Slapstick.".

To make matters worse, the hosts have failed to win any of their five home matches this term, losing four times and drawing once - a goalless stalemate with SC Paderborn on August 29.

Meanwhile, Mauro Lustrinelli's Union have endured a dire campaign so far and are languishing in the relegation zone, but they are far from doomed ahead of their trip to Mainz.

Die Eisernen are presently 17th with seven points after 10 games, level with 16th-placed Schalke in the relegation playoff spot and within three point of Paderborn, FC Koln and Mainz - though their goal-difference makes it improbable for them to climb out of the bottom three this weekend.

Lustrinelli's side were hammered 5-1 by RB Leipzig last Saturday, letting four goals in during a poor second half after heading into the break on level terms thanks to Michel Aebischer's equaliser.

That disappointment extended the Berliners' winless run to six games across all competitions, a stretch that features three defeats and three matches in which they have failed to score.

Saturday's visitors have fared even worse on the road in 2026-27, losing four of their last five away games - each without finding the back of the net - conceding a worrisome 18 goals.

Mainz 05 form (all competitions):.

Union Berlin form (all competitions):.

Mainz will be without the versatile Dominik Kohr this weekend as he continues his recovery from an ankle injury, so expect to see Kacper Potulski, Danny da Costa and Stefan Posch start in Fischer's back three.

Elsewhere, right-sided forward Silas is closing in on return to action after spending eight months out due to a fractured tibia and fibula, though he remains a doubt for Saturday.

If the 28-year-old is unavailable, Sheraldo Becker and Phillip Tietz will start up top, supported by Ransford-Yeboah Konigsdorffer and Nadiem Amiri.

As for Union, they are missing a concerning number of defenders, including centre-backs Zeno Van Den Bosch (suspended for accumulating yellow cards), Stanley Nsoki (calf), and Felix Uduokhai (thigh), not to mention that right-back Josip Juranovic is sidelined due to illness and left-back Andrik Markgraf remains out with a knee injury.

In their absence, Marvin Friedrich and Leopold Querfeld look set to operate at the heart of the visiting backline, flanked by full-backs Christopher Trimmel and Derrick Kohn.

Further forward, wingers Livan Burcu and Robert Skov are both injured, while midfielder Rani Khedira is unavailable after feeling physical discomfort following the loss to RB Leipzig.

Thankfully for the capital club, Kastriot Imeri, Andras Schafer and Michel Aebischer should be on hand to start in the centre of the park, lining up behind Oliver Burke and Andrej Ilic.

Mainz 05 possible starting lineup:.

Zentner; Potulski, Da Costa, Posch; Sano; Caci, Mwene; Konigsdorffer, Amiri; Becker, Tietz.

Union Berlin possible starting lineup:.

Ronnow; Trimmel, Friedrich, Querfeld, Kohn; Kemlein; Imeri, Schafer, Aebischer; Burke, Ilic.

Mainz will be desperate to avoid yet another defeat, and while that aim could be realised against their fellow strugglers, a win seems unlikely due to their dire record on home turf.

Union have been particularly poor on the road this season, and their lacklustre defending means they will realistically need to score at least once to prevent a loss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, juventus captain Manuel Locatelli has called his knee injury one of the hardest spells of his career. Answering questions from young members of the club, he stated his recovery is on track and that he has learned to live with a long wait.

According to recent reports, manuel Locatelli has not played since early September, and the Juventus captain admits the time away has been tough. Speaking in a latest episode of the club’s Junior Reporter series, in which children from the Juventus membership programme interview a first team player, the midfielder was open about how he is coping.

As ANSA reported on Tuesday evening, Locatelli put the injury alongside Italy’s failure to reach the World Cup as the lowest points of his time as a professional.

Sources indicate that locatelli explained that he hurt his knee and now has to stay off the pitch for a long time. He said he feels good and that the work is going well, much of it in the gym rather than on the grass.

“I miss playing football so much, so much, but I have learned to accept this situation,” he told the young reporters, according to the quotes carried by Calciomercato.com. He added that he knows he has to give it time, and that he must do his best to come back in good shape.

On the national team, he did not hide the pain of missing out on the tournament. “When you lose, and lose like that, it is a moment of suffering,” he said.

The problem dates back to 6 September, when Locatelli sprained his right knee in the 1-1 home draw against Milan. Two days later Juventus confirmed in an official medical patch that he had undergone surgery in Lyon to suture the external meniscus. Dr Bertrand Sonnery-Cottet carried out the operation with club doctor Marco Freschi in attendance, and rehabilitation started the following day.

It has been revealed that the club gave no return date at the time. ANSA now says the captain expects to be available again in the first months of 2027, while Football Italia reports that he is not expected back in full training before March.

Locatelli also spoke about leadership. He noted becoming captain was an ambition he had from the moment he arrived from Sassuolo in 2021, and he credited Giorgio Chiellini, Leonardo Bonucci and Danilo for showing him what it means to be present for the group every day. His childhood idols, he said, were Pavel Nedved, Gianluigi Buffon, Alessandro Del Piero and Francesco Totti.

The club tied him down in April, when he signed a fresh contract until June 2030.

His absence has forced Luciano Spalletti to reshape his midfield for most of the autumn, a problem we looked at when Thuram and Locatelli were both missing earlier this month.

Juventus host Omonia in the Europa League on Thursday on the back of a 4-0 win over Venezia, and go to Como on Sunday with a clean bill on the disciplinary front, as covered in our piece on the matchday 12 rulings. Their captain, for now, remains a spectator, but by his own account a patient one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Nsidibe Akpan | 26 Nov 2026 22:39.

Relegation-zone Angers SCO host RC Lens in Ligue 1 on Saturday at Stade Raymond Kopa.

Angers sit 17th on the the Ligue 1 table with eight points after Sunday’s 4-0 defeat at Paris FC, while 11th-placed Lens, on 14 points, are playing under their third head coach of the season.

Les Scoistes have won two of their 11 league games under Stephane Gilli, who replaced Alexandre Dujeux on June 9 after Dujeux resigned and moved to Lorient.

Their last six league results read lost, lost, drawn, lost, lost, lost, a stretch in which Angers have scored three goals and conceded 18.

Angers held Paris FC goalless for the first 46 minutes on Sunday, then conceded four second-half goals, two of them within 10 minutes of the restart.

Gilli returned to Stade Jean Bouin as a former Paris FC head coach, and his proposal to smother their short passing worked only until Patrick Zabi opened the scoring in the 47th minute.

Amine El Ouazzani and Prosper Peter lead the club with two league goals each, and only nine have been scored in 11 games.

Angers have collected four points from six home league games, winning once and drawing once, with a 0-0 draw against Lorient on October 25 the highlight.

Gilli noted after the 2-0 home defeat to Nice on November 8 that he felt he was repeating the same message after every match.

Angers have lost each of their last six Ligue 1 meetings with Lens, including a 5-1 defeat at Stade Bollaert-Delelis on March 20 in which Lanroy Machine scored their only goal.

Les Sang et Or turned to Didier Digard on November 13, three days after sacking interim head coach Yannick Cahuzac, who had replaced Dino Toppmoller on September 15.

Cahuzac lost his job six days after a 9-1 home defeat to Como in the Champions League, a result that still hangs over the squad.

Digard’s first game ended in a 1-1 home draw with Toulouse on November 21, Michael Cuisance equalising from a Thauvin assist, and his first away trip brought a 3-1 defeat at RB Leipzig on Tuesday.

Lens have won four, drawn two and lost five of their 11 league games, scoring 18 and conceding 16, and they have not kept a single clean sheet.

Their 35 goals conceded in all competitions, 16 in the league and 19 in the Champions League, is the worst total among clubs in Europe’s five major leagues.

Their away league record reads one win, one draw and three defeats, the win being a 3-1 victory at Troyes on October 17.

Lens are winless in five games in all competitions, with the last victory a 2-1 home win over Paris FC on October 24.

Florian Thauvin, 33, has five goals and eight assists in the league, and he scored twice in Lens’ 2-1 win at Angers on November 30, 2025.

Opta data showed after Leipzig that Thauvin has lost 15 of his 17 Champions League appearances, and Lens are 33rd in the league phase with three points from five games.

Lens have won their last three visits to Stade Raymond Kopa, by 2-1 in November 2022, 1-0 in August 2024 and 2-1 last season.

Gilli had only two absentees at Wednesday’s training session, goalkeeper Melvin Zinga with a shoulder problem and midfielder Bane Diatta with an ankle injury, while Joseph Kalulu was back after cutting short Tuesday’s session.

Jordan Lefort should return after a one-match suspension, and El Ouazzani is available again after missing two games, which could push Usman Simbakoli, who made his first start of the season at Paris FC, back to the bench.

For the visitors, Ruben Aguilar, hurt against Toulouse, is out alongside Odsonne Edouard, who has had adductor surgery, and Maik Nawrocki, who has a ruptured cruciate ligament.

Cuisance missed the Leipzig game through illness and remains a doubt, while Abdallah Sima, back from a thigh injury, and Ismaelo Ganiou, back from meniscus surgery, are available again.

Angers possible starting lineup:.

Lopes; Arcus, Camara, Lefort, Kalulu; Belkebla, Van den Boomen; Belkhdim, Sbai, El Ouazzani; Peter.

Risser; Todibo, Baidoo, Ganiou; Abdulhamid, Haidara, Titraoui, Udol; Thauvin, Hazard; Sima.

Lens have conceded in all 11 league games this season, so Angers, with El Ouazzani back from injury, should find at least one chance against a defence that has let in 35 goals across all competitions.

Angers have scored only two goals in their last five league games, failing to score in four of them, which is why the hosts are unlikely to take more than one.

The visitors’ away record of one win in five is a genuine concern, but a first league win since October 24 looks the most likely outcome.

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

It has been revealed that emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons.".

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

In a recent development, the study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%.".

According to recent reports, it is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

Industry observers note that while the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

Recent findings suggest that and even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

Premier League officials are 'shocked and furious' after the FA overturned Manchester United defender Leny Yoro's red card at Liverpool - despite the competition's own independent panel unanimously backing the dismissal.

Daily Mail Sport understands that the Premier League's Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel has returned a 5-0 verdict in support of referee Sam Barrott's decision to send off Yoro. The panel also backed VAR's decision not to intervene. Their findings will be released next Wednesday.

But an extraordinary row has now erupted, with United celebrating a successful appeal while the Premier League and refereeing body Pro Ref stand by the original decision.

United appealed against the red card following Sunday's 4-0 defeat at Anfield - Mauricio Pochettino's first game in charge - and an independent FA regulatory commission, consisting of three former players, rescinded Yoro's one-match ban on Tuesday.

In a recent development, the Frenchman was sent off for bringing down Alexander Isak as he ran clear on goal in the eighth minute. United disputed the referee's view that the Liverpool striker would have got to the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens, having taken a heavy touch.

The FA panel appeared to agree, on the basis Yoro did not deny Isak an obvious goalscoring opportunity, meaning the Frenchman is free to play against Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday.

Referee Sam Barrott revealed Manchester United defender Leny Yoro a red card vs Liverpool.

Yoro was sent off for this foul on Alexander Isak - but his red card was overturned on Tuesday.

Barrott and his on-field officiating team from Sunday are believed to be angry at the overturn.

However, top-flight officials are now understood to be demanding answers as to how this has happened, with Pro Ref chief Howard Webb backing his referees.

'That (the red card) was the referee's call, made on the field,' said Webb. 'Then the VAR checks whether the decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect - and formed the opinion it wasn't.

It has been revealed that 'I think by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving swiftly on towards that ball. The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable, I guess. Certainly not clearly wrong.'.

It has been revealed that united sources have branded this interpretation as 'totally wrong' and say it is a process error that fails to interpret the rules properly. They believe that the VAR audio proves there was no meaningful consideration given to challenging Barrott's decision.

United dispute that it was a subjective call and say that it can be proved objectively in a matter of minutes using data that Isak could not have reached the ball before Lammens, even at top speed.

The Premier League and Pro Ref did not comment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, como beat AEK Athens 1-0 to reach 12 points in the Champions League, despite eight unavailable players and a late drop in intensity. Juventus visit the Sinigaglia on Sunday, but must first play Omonia on Thursday.

Recent findings suggest that the narrow victory over AEK was Como’s third straight win in the Champions League. It leaves them close to the knockout stage. It also offers the latest look at Juventus’s next league opponents, on the same ground.

The win came with a stretched squad. Fàbregas told Sky Sport that the absentees were either injured or left out of the Champions League squad list. Making so few changes was, he said, a first in his coaching career. That is a thin bench ahead of a league weekend.

Industry observers note that the scoreline flattered AEK in places. Lucas Da Cunha missed a first-half penalty, and Nico Paz hit the post. At the other end, goalkeeper Robert Sánchez made two important saves before the break. Milla’s goal made him the 11th different player to score for Como in this season’s competition. No other team in the Champions League has had that many different scorers. UEFA named him Player of the Match.

Como had been scoring freely before Matchday 5. On Matchday 4 they won 9-1 away to Lens, a result that put them fourth at the halfway point of the league phase. AEK proved a harder problem. They held Como up for long spells and were difficult to break down.

Industry observers note that the final stretch was the concern. Fabio Capello put it to Fàbregas that Como had dropped off badly in the last 20 minutes. The coach replied that he did not yet have the experience to stay calm in such moments. The late fade is consistent with a group short on fresh legs.

In a recent development, fàbregas also set out his priorities. He noted the win brought Como close to at least a play-off place, but that qualification was not yet secured. In the same breath, he stressed that Serie A matters more to the club. That message points straight at Sunday’s meeting with Juventus.

Juventus have their own European commitment first. Kick-off in Turin, in the Europa League league phase, is at 20:00 UTC. Juve go into that game fifth with 10 points from four matches. Omonia are 18th with six. Sam Barrott of England will referee, with Darren England on VAR.

Recent findings suggest that that schedule cuts into any advantage from Como’s fatigue. Both sides will carry European minutes into the weekend. Juve, however, will have had two fewer days to recover.

In a recent development, the league table adds weight to the fixture. Como sit fourth in Serie A, eight points ahead of Juventus. A home defeat would leave a depleted Como squad with a reduced cushion. A Juve win would close the gap at the end of a demanding week.

Como’s Champions League campaign continues away to Real Betis on 9 December, and the league phase ends with a trip to Barcelona on Wednesday 27 January 2027. After Sunday’s 13th-round meeting at the Sinigaglia, Juventus host Udinese at 18:00 on Sunday 6 December.

  • The Cherries travelled to Vigo with a perfect record in the competition after beating Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, AC Milan and Sparta Prague.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Sully | 26 Nov 2026 22:46, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 22:47.

Bournemouth have become just the third team to win their first five matches in a major European competition.

The Cherries travelled to Vigo with a perfect record in the competition after beating Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, AC Milan and Sparta Prague.

Their impressive record looked set to end when they went a goal and a man down inside the first quarter at Balaidos.

Bournemouth showed character to recover from Bafode Diakite's red card by staging a dramatic second-half turnaround that started with Alvaro Rodriguez's equaliser.

Rayan then netted a 78th-minute winner to fire the Cherries to a 2-1 victory, sending them into an outright lead at the top of the Europa League league phase with the only 100% record out of the 36 teams.

Not only have they significantly boosted their chances of securing a top-eight finish, but the Cherries also became the third team to win their first five games in European competition.

German side Nurnberg were the first team to achieve the feat on their way to reaching the quarter-finals of the 1961-1962 European Cup.

Armenian side Ararat Yerevan replicated the feat when they won the first five games of their UEFA Cup campaign in 1972-1973 before losing on penalties to Kaiserlautern in the last 16.

As well as joining Nurnberg and Ararat in an exclusive group, Bournemouth also became the first Premier League side in three years to win a competitive game after trailing at half time while being a player down.

Prior to Thursday's win, Liverpool were the last team to achieve that feat when Darwin Nunez netted a late brace in a 2-1 victory after Virgil van Dijk had been sent off in the first period.

After winning 10 consecutive games in all competitions for the first time in their history, Bournemouth will now start preparation for Sunday's Premier League meeting with Fulham at Craven Cottage.

Marco Rose's side will then play two more league games against Brighton & Hove Albion and Hull City before they return to Europa League action against Viktoria Plzen on December 10.

Bournemouth head into the weekend in fifth spot in the Premier League table and just three points adrift of fourth-placed Liverpool.

Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 99 min read (19765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~99 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that intratumoural heterogeneity, originating from genetic, epigenetic and phenotypic diversity, is pervasive in cancer and a fundamental barrier to curative treatment1,2.
  • Industry observers note that most cancers comprise genetically, epigenetically and phenotypically diverse cell states within a variable stroma1,2.
  • The intestinal epithelium is sustained by a resident adult stem cell (SC) pool4, which also gives rise to and drives colorectal cancer (CRC).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that intratumoural heterogeneity, originating from genetic, epigenetic and phenotypic diversity, is pervasive in cancer and a fundamental barrier to curative treatment1,2. How these heterogeneous cell states emerge and co-evolve within tumours remains poorly understood. Here we develop a deep-learning framework that quantifies colorectal cancer tissue architecture and nuclear morphology at subcellular resolution to predict patient outcome. Integrating this with spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence and patient-derived organoids, we identify a co-evolutionary relationship between tumour architecture and cancer cell states. We identify architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer that drive cell state diversification by promoting distinct cancer stem cell programmes. Specifically, tissue fragmentation generates compressive forces that activate YAP, suppressing classical stem cell programmes and inducing fetal/regenerative stem cell states that initially manifest as hybrid states with features of partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Subsequent tumour–stroma communication through TGFβ diversifies these into distinct stem cell and EMT states. Reciprocally, β-catenin activity tunes tumour cell responsiveness to architectural cues. Collectively, this work identifies a feedforward loop between cell states and tissue architecture that drives cancer heterogeneity and cell state diversification. Machine-learning-based analyses harness this co-dependency, independently of mutational status or cancer stage, to predict patient outcome.

Industry observers note that most cancers comprise genetically, epigenetically and phenotypically diverse cell states within a variable stroma1,2. A substantial proportion of this heterogeneity arises independently of somatic mutations3 and associates with poor prognosis by diversifying cell states that evade therapy1,2. Whether tissue organization and cell state heterogeneity co-evolve, and how cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic mechanisms interact to drive tumour progression, remain unresolved.

The intestinal epithelium is sustained by a resident adult stem cell (SC) pool4, which also gives rise to and drives colorectal cancer (CRC). During CRC progression, adult SC signatures are depleted while fetal-like/regenerative programmes, which are otherwise present only during development or tissue damage, re-emerge and expand further after metastasis or treatment5,6,7. This plasticity generates extensive heterogeneity and limits therapy responsiveness. Metastatic behaviour requires loss of canonical colonic SC identity, activation of TGFβ and YAP, and acquisition of a fetal-like SC state5,6,7,8.

Genetic drivers of CRC, including BRAF and KRAS mutations and microsatellite instability (MSI), are well established9, but phenotypic plasticity can also arise through epigenetic and transcriptional reprogramming10,11. CRC progression also involves microenvironmental remodelling, including immune infiltration and signalling from cancer-associated fibroblasts12,13,14, together with altered tissue mechanics such as increased extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness and elevated interstitial pressure15,16. These changes are known to alter cell states and promote aggression17,18,19,20. Finally, nuclear shape abnormalities serve as diagnostic indicators of cancer21,22, suggesting that phenotypic heterogeneity is coupled to nuclear organization23,24,25,26. However, how nuclear architecture, tissue organization and cellular heterogeneity are related remains poorly understood.

According to recent reports, here we develop a machine-learning-based image analysis framework to quantify CRC architecture and nuclear morphology, and find that both are highly prognostic independently of mutational status or disease stage. Integrating spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence and patient-derived organoids reveals that distinct tumour architectures associate with specific nuclear morphologies and cell state programmes, and that architecture and phenotypic plasticity co-evolve within individual patients. Mechanistically, tumour fragmentation and associated compressive stress promote transition of LGR5-positive SCs to an ANXA1-positive fetal-like state through YAP, whereas ECM composition and stromal TGFβ signalling promote EMT. These findings reveal a feedforward loop between tissue architecture, nuclear shape and cell state diversification that drives poor outcome in CRC.

In a recent development, to investigate the relationship between nuclear morphology, tissue architecture and disease outcome, we obtained pathologist-curated tumour microarrays (TMAs) from 1,342 patients with CRC with complete clinical information (Extended Data Fig. 1a). TMA punches were taken from primary tumour resection specimens at paired tumour core (CT; 1,834 cores) and invasive margin (IM; 1,502 cores) locations (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1b). The slides were stained for the epithelial marker pan-cadherin (pan-EPI) to identify tumour cell boundaries and to separate tumour from stroma, and with DAPI to mark all nuclei (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1c). Nuclei were segmented at single-cell resolution27 (over 25 million cells) to derive quantitative descriptors of nuclear shape, size and deformation (Fig. 1b). Patients with MSI and microsatellite-stable (MSS) patients were analysed separately.

a, Representative images of CRC TMA samples stained with DAPI from the CT and IM regions. The yellow rectangles indicate the magnified areas (bottom). The dashed line demarcates tumour (T) and stroma (S). Scale bars, 500 µm (top) and 25 µm (bottom). b, Schematic of nuclear morphometry parameters extracted from single-cell nuclear segmentation. Scale bars, 5 μm. c, Pearson correlation matrix of nuclear morphometry features across all single cells from the CT and IM. d, Univariate Cox proportional hazard analysis of patient-averaged nuclear morphometrics for disease-specific survival in MSS patients. The x axis reveals the log hazard ratio with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the CT (blue; n = 773 patients) and IM (pink; n = 484 patients). A patient is counted in a compartment only when that compartment has a nuclear-morphometry average and a survival time. Nuclear circularity is the strongest indicator of poor survival. P values were calculated using Wald tests. e, Schematic of the tumour architecture classification pipeline. TMA cores with homogeneous architecture were used to train a U-Net and generate feature embeddings (blue, solid (sol.); yellow, glandular (gland.); red, fragmented (frag.)). Individual cores were subdivided into tiles and classified locally; the dominant architecture (more than 50% of tiles) determined the overall classification. f, The average stromal, tumour cell neighbourhood and tissue morphology descriptors across architecture types for CT (left) and IM (right). c.o.v., coefficient of variation. g, Representative TMA cores with homogeneous architectures showing classifier predictions (top), projection of three closest neighbours by distance (middle) and relative cell alignment (bottom). Scale bars, 400 µm. h, Kaplan–Meier curves for disease-specific survival of MSS patients, all stages, stratified by architecture type in the CT (n = 967) and IM (n = 871), mixed included (pairwise log-rank tests with glandular architecture as the reference (ref) group). An architecture label is sufficient for inclusion, which is why n is larger than in d. Stage II–III curves are in Extended Data Fig. 3c. i,j, Representative images of pan-cadherin and DAPI staining (i) and quantification of nuclear shape parameters (j) across architecture groups in the CT. n = 1,402 cores with both an architecture class and a nuclear measurement, not 1,402 patients. Scale bars, 50 µm. Statistical analysis was performed using patient-level permutation tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. The box plots show the median (centre lines), 25th–75th percentile (interquartile range (IQR); box limits) and 1.5 × IQR (whiskers).

Industry observers note that to identify the most informative nuclear morphology parameters, we computed pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients across single cells (Fig. 1c). Clustering revealed two principal parameter modules. The first captured nuclear deformation and irregularity: elliptic Fourier coefficient (EFC) ratio28 and solidity described deviations from a perfect oval at multiple spatial scales, whereas circularity and aspect ratio captured larger-scale deformations (Fig. 1b,c). The second captured nuclear size, including area and axis ratio (Fig. 1c). Parameters were averaged per patient and tumour region. In MSS patients, univariate Cox models of these averages showed that nuclear shape, more consistently than nuclear size, was associated with disease-specific survival: patients with rounder, smoother nuclei (higher circularity, solidity and EFC ratio, and lower aspect ratio) had poorer survival (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1d; CT n = 773, IM n = 484). Multivariate models incorporating age, stage, tumour localization and Immunoscore29 confirmed this association in stage II–III but not stage I disease (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Nuclear circularity also correlated with tumour stage (Extended Data Fig. 1d–g).

This association prompted us to examine whether nuclear morphology reflects local tissue architecture. Histopathological inspection of the pan-EPI signal identified six predominant, quantifiable architecture types: well-polarized, tightly packed glands (termed glandular); glandular structures with emergent branches and minor stromal infiltrations (glandular infiltrated); densely packed glands with loss of polarity and minimal stromal contact (solid); an intermediate glandular-solid phenotype (glandular dense); gland-like structures with detaching cell clusters (moderately fragmented); and poorly differentiated glands with high stromal infiltration and disrupted continuity (fragmented; Extended Data Fig. 1h).

In a recent development, we then established a quantitative workflow to classify the architectural distribution within each TMA sample into three groups: glandular (consolidating glandular, glandular dense and glandular infiltrated), solid and fragmented (consolidating moderately and highly fragmented). A U-Net convolutional neural network was trained on samples with homogeneous, archetypal architectures to learn architecture-specific tissue embeddings (Fig. 1e). TMA cores were subdivided into tiles, and a classifier trained on these embeddings predicted the architecture type/tile (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). The proportion of tiles within each category defined an overall architecture score/patient, where the specific architecture exceeding 50% of tiles designated the dominant type. Mixed classification was assigned in cases in which no single architecture reached this threshold.

Architecture classifications were validated against quantitative, interpretable histological features including lumen area, tumour–stroma interface roughness, cell density and cell–cell alignment (Fig. 1f,g and Extended Data Fig. 2d). The 196 cores selected as architectural archetypes formed significantly tighter, better-separated clusters in morphological feature space compared with size-matched random draws from the cohort (Extended Data Fig. 2e), confirming their representativeness.

According to recent reports, notably, the tissue architecture at both the CT and IM was highly predictive of patient outcome (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Patients with dominant fragmented architectures indicated the least favourable prognosis (Fig. 1h). Fragmented cores were modestly more prevalent in patients with stage III/IV CRC (Extended Data Fig. 3b), but architecture retained independent prognostic value within the stage II/III subgroups (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Architecture was not prognostic in the MSI subset (Extended Data Fig. 3d), consistent with the distinct pathophysiology of this CRC subtype. The prognostic value of architecture in MSS patients was independently validated in a second cohort of 270 patients (Extended Data Fig. 3e,f).

Analysis of spatial concordance revealed that nearly all patients with fragmented tumour cores also displayed fragmented IMs, whereas the reverse did not hold: a substantial proportion of solid or glandular cores presented with fragmented IMs (Extended Data Fig. 3g,h). This asymmetry suggests that tumour fragmentation originates at the IM before propagating to the tumour core.

Industry observers note that to contextualize these architecture classifications within established histopathological criteria, we compared fragmentation with tumour budding, an established clinical marker of aggressiveness30. High budding grades (BD2/3) were more frequent in patients with fragmented architectures, indicating partial correspondence between structural disintegration and budding morphology (Extended Data Fig. 4a). However, fragmented architecture retained prognostic value even among patients with low budding scores (BD1; Extended Data Fig. 4b). As budding is classically quantified at the IM, but has also been reported to occur within the tumour core31, an expert pathologist separately scored intratumoural budding from the tumour cores of fragmented TMAs. Most fragmented tumour cores did not score positive for budding, and budding score correlated only weakly with degree of fragmentation (Extended Data Fig. 4c), demonstrating that fragmentation and budding capture distinct features. The signet ring cell histological subtype was predominantly classified as fragmented, consistent with its structural characteristics (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Fragmented architecture was more prevalent in high-grade tumours but also detected in low-grade disease, and remained prognostic in both groups (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f). Notably, 45% of samples classified as both high-grade and high-budding lacked fragmented architecture (Extended Data Fig. 4g), and fragmentation remained an independent predictor of outcome in patients with stage II/III CRC after controlling for both budding grade and histological grade (Extended Data Fig. 4h). Finally, fragmented architectures occurred in both colon and rectal tumours and did not correlate with Immunoscore (Extended Data Fig. 4i,j). Thus, fragmentation captures tumour features that are not encompassed by budding, grading or Immunoscore.

Consistent with the initial hypothesis that single-nucleus morphology reflects local tissue architecture, tumour regions with glandular or solid architectures were enriched for elongated nuclei. Regions with fragmented architecture were dominated by rounder, more-regular nuclei (Fig. 1i,j and Extended Data Fig. 4k). Thus, tumour architecture is a strong independent prognostic indicator in CRC, and round, regular nuclei probably reflect the fragmented tissue context.

It has been revealed that to mechanistically dissect the relationship between nuclear shape, tissue architecture and patient outcome, we performed spatial transcriptomics (GeoMx DSP) on eight whole-tumour resection samples from the same patient cohort (Fig. 2a). For each patient, 10–50 regions of interest spanning the full spectrum of architectural diversity were selected and the transcriptomes of tumour epithelium and surrounding stroma profiled separately (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 5a). Leiden clustering defined transcriptional clusters with distinct molecular profiles (Fig. 2b,c). Although transcriptomes were highly patient specific, transcriptional clusters within each patient were spatially organized into discrete domains corresponding to distinct tumour architectures (Fig. 2b–d and Extended Data Fig. 5b–f), suggesting that architecture associates with specific cell states.

In a recent development, a, Schematic of the experimental design. b, Representative images of pan-EPI, αSMA and CD45 staining of whole patient tumours to identify tumour and stroma for selection of regions of interest (marked by the numbered rectangles). Examples of two patients out of eight (patient 8 and patient 5) are shown. The numbers indicate the corresponding magnified regions, and the colours indicate the corresponding molecular clusters. Scale bars, 5 mm (white) and 100 µm (black). c, Leiden clusters of all patient samples annotated by patient identity (top) or molecular identity (bottom). d, The distribution of tumour architectures across molecular clusters. e, Gene set enrichment analyses of SC marker genes across tumour architectures. coreHRC, core high-relapse cancer/high-risk clone signature; ISC, intestinal stem cell; revCSC, revival cancer stem cell; RSC, regenerative stem cell. Note the enrichment of CBC marker genes in glandular architectures and regenerative SC and high relapse gene signatures in moderately/highly fragmented architectures. f, Quantification of selected key SC marker gene expression levels across the tumour architectures. n = 249 tumour areas of interest (AOIs) from 8 patients. Tumour AOIs were collected from the ROIs, not the drawn ROIs themselves (see Methods). Statistical analysis was performed using two-sided patient-stratified permutation tests accounting for repeated tumour AOIs; Benjamini–Hochberg correction was applied across markers. NS, not significant. g, Gene set enrichment analysis of EMT marker genes across tumour architectures. Note the enrichment of EMT marker genes in moderately (mod.)/highly fragmented architectures. h, Quantification of selected key EMT marker gene expression levels across tumour architectures. Statistical testing was performed as described in f. i, The distribution of tumour phenotypes across tissue architectures within the CT and IM. Note the enrichment of regenerative (reg) and EMT states in fragmented architectures. j, Kaplan–Meier curve of disease-specific survival for MSS CT patients with both an architecture class and a multiplex immunofluorescence phenotype (n = 653). Figure 1h includes every MSS CT patient with an architecture label (n = 967), including patients without a multiplex phenotype. Note the poor survival of patients with combined tumour fragmentation and regenerative/EMT states. Statistical analysis was performed using pairwise log-rank tests versus the glandular-differentiated (diff) high reference group. The box plots show the median (centre lines), IQR (box limits) and 1.5 × IQR (whiskers). NES, normalized enrichment score.

To test this, we scored each architecture type for enrichment of known cell state signatures. Using published gene sets for classical LGR5-positive crypt base columnar SCs (CBCs) and LGR5-negative regenerative/fetal-like SC populations8,14,32,33,34, we found that moderately and highly fragmented architectures were enriched for regenerative/fetal-like programmes, whereas classical CBC signatures were enriched in glandular architectures (Fig. 2e,f and Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). EMT is a further hallmark of malignant progression, co-opted from developmental and wound-healing programmes to facilitate tumour cell dissemination35. Moderately and highly fragmented architectures were strongly enriched for published EMT signatures (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 5i). Thus, glandular and solid architectures associate with the classical CBC state, while fragmented architectures associate with fetal/regenerative SC programmes and EMT.

According to recent reports, to determine whether the transcriptional signatures correspond to distinct cellular phenotypes, and to validate the relationship between cell states and architecture at scale, we applied multiplex immunofluorescence to the initial TMA cohort. MSS patient samples were stained with a panel of antibodies targeting CBC, fetal/regenerative SC, EMT and proliferative states (Methods). Single cells were segmented and clustered based on combined marker expression36 and closely related phenotypic clusters were consolidated into seven major phenotypes (Extended Data Fig. 6a). These comprised differentiated tumour cell states with varying expression levels of CDX2 and PROX1, a transcriptional repressor induced in the fetal/regenerative state that suppresses non-intestinal lineage genes to enable phenotypic plasticity8. We also detected a highly proliferative population that retained CDX2 expression. Moreover, annexin-A1 (ANXA1)-positive cells and vimentin (VIM)-positive tumour cells formed two distinct populations. ANXA1-positive cells showed increased levels of tenascin-C (TNC), a hallmark ECM protein defining the EMT programme (Extended Data Figs. 6a–c and 7a). This indicated that EMT-related features might manifest as partially overlapping programmes across phenotypic subsets rather than within a single discrete state.

Recent findings suggest that we next examined the distribution of these phenotypes across tumour architectures and confirmed that fragmented regions were enriched in regenerative and VIM-positive EMT-like populations, whereas other architectures were preferentially associated with differentiated tumour cell states (Fig. 2i). Notably, fragmented architecture was not exclusively composed of regenerative or EMT-like populations, but also included areas dominated by well-differentiated or proliferative tumour cell states, indicative of state heterogeneity. Conversely, glandular architecture was not exclusively composed of differentiated cells, but also contained clusters of regenerative tumour cells (Fig. 2i and Extended Data Fig. 7a).

This partial overlap prompted us to examine whether specific architecture–cell-state combinations carried distinct prognostic information. Stratifying patients by tumour cell phenotype composition revealed that the combination of fragmented architecture and regenerative phenotype was associated with the worst survival, most prominently in the tumour core (Fig. 2j and Extended Data Fig. 7b,c), whereas cell phenotype composition alone was not predictive of outcome in CT (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Patients with fragmented regenerative tumour cores predominantly also displayed this signature at the IM, whereas the reverse was less frequent (Extended Data Fig. 7e), consistent with the state originating at the IM and propagating towards the tumour core. Collectively, combining architectural and phenotypic information provides a prognostic signature superior to either modality alone.

The tight association between cell states and tissue architecture raised the possibility that tumour architectures, like cell states, undergo dynamic transitions during cancer progression. Given that moderately and highly fragmented architectures were enriched for both EMT and regenerative SC states, we first examined whether these programmes co-exist within the same cells or define distinct populations. To assess the potential existence of hybrid EMT/regenerative states and their subsequent diversification, we mined two CRC single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets12,37. Subclustering of MSS patient tumour epithelial cells and GSEA analysis for CBC, EMT and regenerative SC signatures revealed that EMT and regenerative signatures were enriched within the same Leiden clusters in both datasets, while CBC signatures occupied separate clusters (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d). Examination of individual cells both within specific clusters and across the full dataset identified a substantial population with high co-enrichment of EMT and regenerative signatures, indicative of a hybrid state (Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). Co-expression of key marker genes including VIM, SNAI1 (encoding SNAIL1), ANXA1 and EMP1 in single cells further supported the existence of this hybrid state (Extended Data Fig. 8g). CBC signatures were not correlated with regenerative SC signatures, suggesting that cells must exit the CBC state before acquiring hybrid identity (Extended Data Fig. 8e,f).

According to recent reports, diffusion pseudotime analysis of a subclustered dataset encompassing CBC, regenerative and EMT states (clusters 0, 3, 4 and 6), initiated from the most stem-like cluster identified by CytoTRACE scoring38, revealed a trajectory from CBC towards a hybrid EMT/regenerative population. This trajectory was characterized by progressive downregulation of CBC and stemness-associated transcription factors ASCL2 and HMGA1 and the identity marker LGR5, followed by upregulation of regenerative SC markers and plasticity-associated KLF family transcription factors and, ultimately, upregulation of EMT transcription factors including SMAD3 and other established EMT markers39,40,41 (Extended Data Fig. 8h–j).

Industry observers note that to spatially resolve the distribution of regenerative and EMT states within tumour tissue, we integrated spatial transcriptomics with single-cell resolution multiplex immunofluorescence across whole-tumour sections, using ANXA1 as a regenerative state marker and VIM, SNAIL1 and E-cadherin/pan-cadherin ratio as EMT markers. ANXA1-positive cells were highly enriched in fragmented regions (Fig. 3a–c and Extended Data Fig. 9a), consistent with the transcriptomic data. At the tumour–stroma boundary of moderately fragmented regions, ANXA1-positive cells also exhibited EMT features, confirming co-existence of regenerative and EMT programmes at this interface (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). However, within fragmented regions, cells with high VIM expression were spatially segregated from ANXA1high cells, forming largely non-overlapping, spatially proximal populations (Fig. 3c,d and Extended Data Fig. 9d). SNAIL1 indicated comparable expression across both populations (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 9a,c), consistent with a transcriptional continuum rather than binary state switching. The predominantly mutually exclusive but spatially proximal distribution of ANXA1high and VIMhigh cells suggests plasticity between regenerative SC and EMT states.

We next used trajectory analyses of the spatial transcriptomes to infer the most probable routes of architecture transitions during CRC progression. Glandular architectures demonstrated highest probability of transitioning to moderately fragmented, while solid architectures preferentially transitioned to highly fragmented (Fig. 3e). To control for potential confounding by unequal architecture representation across patients, we performed pseudotime analysis within individual patients with heterogeneous architecture distributions, using a central glandular region as the reference point and grouping regions by nearest neighbour to account for spatial proximity effects. Architecture and spatial cluster distributions within each pseudotime window were consistent near both start and end points across all three patients analysed (Fig. 3f–h and Extended Data Fig. 9e), and key CBC, regenerative and EMT marker genes showed monotonic changes along the pseudotime trajectory (Fig. 3i), indicating that architecture transitions are accompanied by corresponding changes in cell state. These transitions were recapitulated in the U-Net tile embedding space combined with multiplex immunofluorescence-based cell state classification, in which the strongest connections were found between glandular and solid architectures, and between solid and fragmented architectures, whereby transition of glandular to solid architectures corresponded to a transition from differentiated and PROX1high states to regenerative and EMT states (Extended Data Fig. 9f).

Together, these analyses demonstrate that cell states and tissue architectures co-evolve within individual patients, and that EMT and regenerative programmes form a continuum, distinct from the CBC state, which can diversify towards regenerative SC or EMT-dominant identities.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate the mechanism driving architecture-linked cell state diversification, we first examined whether the distinct nuclear morphologies observed across architectures in whole-tumour resections reflected the same co-evolutionary relationship seen in the TMAs. Single-cell segmentation and quantitative nuclear morphology analyses confirmed that glandular architectures associated with nuclear elongation while fragmented architectures associated with increased circularity (Extended Data Fig. 10a), consistent with the TMA findings. We next examined microenvironmental signals potentially driving this transition. Spatial transcriptomic scoring of the tumour compartment revealed elevated TGFβ pathway activity and higher YAP transcriptional programme scores in fragmented architectures (Fig. 4a,b), and immunofluorescence confirmed increased nuclear YAP levels in these regions (Fig. 4c). Analysis of paired stromal compartments showed that fragmented regions were additionally enriched for T cell, natural killer cell and myeloid cell transcriptional signatures (Extended Data Fig. 10b). Collagen architecture in fragmented regions was characterized by increased structural complexity and reduced fibre coherence, and TNC showed similar, albeit less pronounced, architectural variation (Fig. 4d). Thus, fragmented architectures show coordinated stromal and ECM remodelling and elevated tumour cell TGFβ and YAP activity, consistent with an altered mechanical microenvironment.

To examine causative relationships between changes in the ECM mechanical microenvironment, YAP and cell states, we turned to disease modelling using patient-derived organoids that were whole-genome sequenced and validated to contain APC and TP53 mutations. A shallow scRNA-seq analysis revealed that, like the in vivo tumours, the organoids also displayed hybrid EMT/regenerative SC states and mutually exclusive classic CBC and regenerative SC states (Extended Data Fig. 11a,b). We then examined whether changes in architecture could promote transition from a classic CBC to hybrid or diversified cell states. To this end we selected two independent patient-derived CRC organoid lines that, based on the scRNA-seq data, had high levels of classic LGR5/OLFM4 CBCs and only low levels of ANXA1/PLAUR regenerative SCs (lines 1 and 2; Extended Data Fig. 11a,c). We plated these two lines onto engineered colonic sheets42, where cells could grow unrestricted on flat surfaces or be confined in finger-like protruding channels (Fig. 4e–g). Analysis of RNA levels using in situ hybridization showed heterogeneous cell phenotypes with regions enriched for ANXA1high cells that were distinct from LGR5high cells (Fig. 4e). Notably, ANXA1high cells were enriched at bottoms of the confined finger-like channels whereas LGR5high cells showed no preferential localization (Fig. 4e). EMT states as marked by VIM expression were homogeneously low and distributed within the channels with partial overlap with ANXA1high cells (Fig. 4e).

Notably, while both patient lines responded to the architectures, the response of line 2 was stronger than line 1 (Fig. 4e,f). Examination of differences between these lines in the scRNA-seq data revealed that, while both lines when grown in Matrigel contained high levels of classic LGR5/OLFM4-positive SCs and low levels of ANXA1/PLAUR-positive regenerative SCs, line 2 revealed a more prominent signature of β-catenin activity (Extended Data Fig. 11d), which is central to the regulation of stemness and EMT in the colon43,44. This was associated with high expression of the β-catenin target gene and plasticity transcription factor SOX48,40 (Extended Data Fig. 11c,d). Consistent with its elevated β-catenin transcriptional signature, high nuclear β-catenin was seen only in line 2 cells (Fig. 4f,g). Moreover, while YAP1 expression was not substantially different between the lines, line 2 showed higher baseline activity, as indicated by an enriched YAP transcriptional signature (Extended Data Fig. 11c,d). However, within this line, nuclear β-catenin was seen only in the unrestricted, flat areas of the engineered sheets, while it was undetectable in the channels enriched in ANXA1high cells (Fig. 4f,g). This implied that, while intrinsically high β-catenin activity correlated with the responsiveness to tissue architecture, potentially through promoting SOX4 expression, confinement of cells into channels suppressed WNT activity and promoted the emergence of an ANXA1-positive cell state. The role of β-catenin activity in tuning the responsiveness to mechanosignalling was confirmed by culturing the responsive line 2 in the presence or absence of Chir-99021 to activate canonical WNT. Upregulation of AXIN2 and the key CBC marker ASCL2 expression, as well as elevated SOX4 and β-catenin levels in the nucleus in response to β-catenin stabilization by Chir-99021 confirmed that these cells indeed were responsive to WNT manipulation despite their APC mutation (Extended Data Fig. 11e–h), consistent with previous studies45,46. Importantly, pretreatment with Chir-99021 enhanced the impact of YAP activation on ANXA1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 11i), indicating that high β-catenin/SOX4 state enhances mechanoresponsiveness.

To test whether mechanical compression was sufficient to promote SC fate transitions through YAP activation, we cultured the patient organoids in Matrigel, in which ANXA1 levels were initially low, and then subjected the organoids to mechanical compression47 (Fig. 4h,i and Extended Data Fig. 11c). Indeed, confining the organoids was sufficient to trigger emergence of ANXA1/PLAUR-positive cells with corresponding suppression of LGR5/OLFM4-positive cells (Fig. 4h). Importantly, confinement also activated YAP (Fig. 4i). However, confinement was not sufficient to promote a diversified EMT state (Extended Data Fig. 11j,k). Collectively, these data suggest that architecture-derived mechanical signals deplete the CBC state and induce a regenerative SC state but are insufficient to promote EMT, and that high nuclear β-catenin and SOX4 expression enhances the efficiency of CBC-to-regenerative SC transition.

According to recent reports, having earlier established that SMAD3 expression is correlated with progression towards EMT, while YAP activation is associated with mechanically driven regenerative SC states, we investigated whether the TGFβ1 and YAP pathways cooperate to drive cell-state diversification. Patient organoids (line 2) were treated with a LATS kinase inhibitor (TDI-011536)48 to activate YAP, recombinant TGFβ1 or both for 4 days, and then analysed using scRNA-seq. YAP activation triggered robust transcriptional state changes, whereas TGFβ1 alone had more-limited effects (Fig. 5a,b and Extended Data Fig. 12a). Benchmarking cell states against a previously published dataset37, which is enriched in regenerative state cells, showed that YAP activation depleted the CBC state (Fig. 5c,d), consistent with observations from the mechanical compression experiments and with CBC depletion in regenerative state cells in vivo49. YAP activation also shifted the hybrid state towards the regenerative pole of the regenerative SC-to-EMT continuum (Fig. 5b–d and Extended Data Fig. 12b). TGFβ1 alone modestly expanded the hybrid state and moderately induced EMT transcription factor expression, while combined treatment drove more robust diversification of the hybrid state into two distinct populations (Fig. 5a–d and Extended Data Fig. 12a,b).
